questions.question: What is the objective of the Majuli virtual reality tour case study?
options: To capture tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage and digitally preserve it through an immersive experience because the island is disappearing.
To collect end-user data through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire in the evaluation study.
To analyze participant responses and symptoms of cyber sickness to identify potential areas for improvement.
To measure user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment and identify potential improvement areas.
questions.explanation: The case study's objective is to capture Majuli's tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage and digitally preserve it through an immersive experience, because the island is disappearing.

questions.question: Which usability aspects are the stated focus of the Majuli VR tour evaluation?
options: User engagement, presence, and comfort
User engagement, comfort, and satisfaction
User engagement, presence, and cyber sickness
Presence, comfort, and learning performance
questions.explanation: The evaluation aims to measure usability aspects specifically as user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment.

questions.question: How did the Majuli VR tour evaluation collect data from end users?
options: Through informal interviews and open-ended observations of participant behavior.
Through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire, with responses collected subjectively, objectively, or both.
Only through a structured questionnaire that measured objective behavioral data.
Only through a controlled experiment that recorded subjective participant feedback.
questions.explanation: Data were collected through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire, and participant responses could be subjective, objective, or both.

questions.question: What can the structured questionnaire in the Majuli VR tour evaluation be used for?
options: It can only collect subjective data through a rating scale.
It can measure objective data or behavioral data, and sometimes collect data through a rating scale.
It can only measure objective data from a controlled experiment.
It can only record presence on a standard presence questionnaire.
questions.explanation: The structured questionnaire was related to the evaluation research question and could measure objective or behavioral data, or sometimes collect data through a rating scale.

questions.question: In the Majuli VR tour evaluation, what user categories did the participant groups correspond to?
options: Students, gamers, and real estate users
Healthcare users, educators, and tourists
Pilgrims, tourists, and healthcare users
Pilgrims, students, and tourists
questions.explanation: The participants were divided into three groups corresponding to the tour system's supported user categories: pilgrims, students, and tourists.

questions.question: How was the VR tour system configured for the participants?
options: A Meta Quest 2 HMD connected to a PC through Oculus Link
A Meta Quest 2 HMD used standalone without a PC
A Meta Quest 2 HMD connected to a PC without using Oculus Link
A Meta Quest 2 HMD connected to a smartphone through a wireless link
questions.explanation: The system was developed for the Meta Quest 2 HMD, and the HMD was connected to a personal computer via an enabled Oculus Link.

questions.question: Which participant characteristic could bias the Majuli VR tour evaluation output?
options: Most participants were unfamiliar with joystick controllers
Most participants had prior virtual reality experience
Most participants had abnormal uncorrected vision
Most participants had no prior virtual reality experience
questions.explanation: Twenty-one of the twenty-seven participants had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output.

questions.question: What type of controller familiarity did all Majuli VR tour evaluation participants have?
options: They had used only a gamepad in a VR or non-VR context
They had used a joystick-based controller in a VR or non-VR context
They had used only a mouse and keyboard in a VR or non-VR context
They had used only a touchscreen in a VR or non-VR context
questions.explanation: All participants were familiar with the joystick-based controller and with controller-based interaction, having used that type of controller in a virtual or non-virtual reality context.

questions.question: What kind of questionnaire was the QEP in the Majuli VR tour assessment?
options: A virtual tourism enjoyment rating form
A revised standard sickness questionnaire
A revised standard presence questionnaire
A standard headset compatibility checklist
questions.explanation: Presence is measured by standard questionnaires, and the QEP was a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire used to measure presence.

questions.question: What numeric range was used for QEP responses?
options: From 0 to 3
From 0 to 19
From 1 to 7
From 1 to 19
questions.explanation: Responses to the QEP questionnaire were recorded on a Likert scale ranging from 1 to 7.

questions.question: Why was the simulator sickness questionnaire used in the Majuli VR tour assessment?
options: It was a standard and popular cyber sickness measure, though not originally developed for cyber sickness
It was originally developed for measuring cyber sickness in immersive experiences
It was a 2004 revision of the standard presence questionnaire
It recorded QEP presence responses on a 1-to-7 Likert scale
questions.explanation: The simulator sickness questionnaire was used to measure cyber sickness because it is standard and popular for that purpose, even though it was not originally developed for cyber sickness.

questions.question: What did a rating of 0 on the simulator sickness questionnaire indicate?
options: Mild symptoms only
A moderate sickness score
No symptoms
The most severe symptoms
questions.explanation: Participants rated their cyber sickness symptoms from 0 to 3, where 0 meant no symptoms and 3 meant the most severe symptoms.

questions.question: Why were SSQ scores computed before and after exposure?
options: To determine whether the virtual tour matched an earlier in-person visit
To calculate a 1-to-7 QEP presence score
To compare them and assess the design's effect on sickness scores
To measure the total number of optional sound items in the QEP
questions.explanation: The SSQ scores were computed before and after exposure and compared to get an idea of the effect of the Majuli VR tour assessment design on those scores.

questions.question: What problem can a brief pre-experiment training session help reduce in a virtual reality experiment?
options: Pre-exposure simulator sickness
The amount of heritage information obtained
The need to prepare hardware and software
Familiarity or prior-experience bias
questions.explanation: The training demonstrates the system's features and how to use them, bringing participants to the same level and reducing or nullifying familiarity or prior-experience bias.

questions.question: In a virtual reality tour evaluation, which questionnaire was completed after exploration to measure presence?
options: The simulator sickness questionnaire completed before exploration
The simulator sickness questionnaire completed after the session
A pre-experiment training checklist
The presence questionnaire
questions.explanation: Participants completed the presence questionnaire after exploration, while the simulator sickness questionnaire was used before and after exposure as cybersickness measures.

questions.question: Why was the exploration time for the virtual reality tour estimated from pilot studies, trials, and literature?
options: To standardize the presence questionnaire response scale
To calculate the total sickness score after exposure
To allow enough exploration while minimizing exposure-related cybersickness
To choose the hardware and software for the setup
questions.explanation: The time was chosen to give users sufficient time to explore the large island and obtain heritage information while minimizing cybersickness, which depends on exposure.

questions.question: In a standard controlled experiment, which stage specifically addresses bias?
options: Preparing hardware, software, and questionnaires
Completing the simulator sickness questionnaire before exposure
Defining a procedure that eliminates possible biases
Defining the users and identifying participants
questions.explanation: An important stage in a standard controlled experiment is to define a procedure that eliminates possibilities of biases.

questions.question: How did each participant take part in the virtual reality tour evaluation?
options: By exploring one section with a group
By watching a guided demo of the tour
By completing the tour through a remote presentation
By exploring the entire tour individually in a controlled setting
questions.explanation: Each participant individually explored the entire tour in a controlled setting.

questions.question: Which presence measure was additionally reported only for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island?
options: Tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity
Interface quality of the tour
Involvement in the virtual tour
Visual fidelity of the island
questions.explanation: The presence measure included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity for all participants. Tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

questions.question: How were the overall presence results for the Majuli VR tour interpreted?
options: Good presence: users felt perfectly located in the virtual environment.
Low presence: users felt only weakly located in the virtual environment.
Poor presence: users felt disconnected from the virtual environment.
Good presence: users felt reasonably well located in the virtual environment.
questions.explanation: The overall presence results were summarized as good presence, meaning users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

questions.question: What did the more favorable presence opinions of participants who had previously visited Majuli Island indicate?
options: Their favorable opinions indicated that the system only resembled the island visually, not in interaction or implementation.
Their higher expectations made them perceive the digital avatar as farther from reality than the tour was for other participants.
They were more comfortable with digital exploration and perceived the system as closely mimicking the physical island.
They were less comfortable with digital exploration and perceived the system as failing to mimic the physical island.
questions.explanation: Previous visitors’ more favorable opinions, despite higher expectations, indicated greater comfort with digital exploration and that the system reasonably mimicked the physical island in design, interaction, and implementation, with the digital avatar close to reality.

questions.question: What conclusion was supported by the statistically significant difference between users with and without prior exposure to digital or virtual tours?
options: Prior exposure to such systems harms users’ overall experience.
Prior exposure to Majuli Island itself helps users gain a better experience.
Prior exposure to such systems helps users gain a better experience.
Prior exposure to such systems has no effect on users’ experience.
questions.explanation: The Welch t-test revealed a statistically significant difference between users with prior exposure to digital or virtual tours and users without such exposure, supporting the conclusion that prior exposure helps users gain a better experience.

questions.question: What cybersickness measures were collected for the Majuli virtual tour?
options: Pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor effects, and total severity
Pre- and post-exposure hardware latency and visual fidelity ratings
Pre- and post-exposure QEP data for involvement, interface quality, and visual fidelity
Post-exposure SSQ data only for nausea, disorientation, and total severity
questions.explanation: The Majuli virtual tour cybersickness evaluation used the SSQ and collected both pre-exposure and post-exposure data for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor effects, and total severity.

questions.question: What does a small pre- to post-exposure difference in nausea and disorientation suggest about the Majuli virtual tour?
options: It suggests that the tour caused strong nausea and disorientation
It suggests that oculomotor severity was the only measured cybersickness item
It suggests that the tour did not generally induce cybersickness
It suggests that total sickness and oculomotor severity showed no difference
questions.explanation: The average pre- and post-exposure SSQ box plots showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the tour did not generally induce cybersickness.

questions.question: Which SSQ outcomes showed a statistically significant difference between pre-exposure and post-exposure in the Majuli virtual tour evaluation?
options: The nausea and oculomotor outcomes
The nausea and disorientation outcomes
The oculomotor and total sickness outcomes
The disorientation and total sickness outcomes
questions.explanation: The statistical test on the pre- and post-exposure SSQ data revealed a significant difference for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item.

questions.question: What does a statistically significant pre- to post-exposure change in total sickness indicate about the Majuli virtual tour?
options: That participant age was the only cause of the change
That the tour design removed all cybersickness from the experience
That the tour design had some effect on total sickness
That the tour design had no effect on total sickness
questions.explanation: The significant pre- to post-exposure change in total sickness indicates that the Majuli virtual tour design had some effect on total sickness.

questions.question: What did the presence measure mostly indicate in the evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality tour?
options: No meaningful presence results.
Mostly poor presence results.
Presence results limited to users without prior experience.
Mostly good presence results.
questions.explanation: The presence measure gave mostly good results in the evaluation of the Majuli VR Tour.

questions.question: What did the evaluation suggest about users with prior experience in the Majuli virtual reality tour?
options: They may show no difference in presence results from users without prior experience.
They may find the tour less acceptable than users without prior experience.
They may show worse presence results because their expectations are higher.
They may find the tour more acceptable and may show better presence results.
questions.explanation: Prior experience may lead to even better results, with users with prior experience possibly finding the VR Tour more acceptable than users without prior experience.

questions.question: Which cybersickness component was reported as possibly affected in the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?
options: The oculomotor component, which may lead to some effect on total sickness.
The total sickness item, which may lead to some effect on oculomotor severity.
The nausea component, which may lead to some effect on total sickness.
The disorientation component, which may lead to some effect on total sickness.
questions.explanation: Certain cybersickness items were not found to affect severity, but the oculomotor component may be affected and may lead to some effect on total sickness.

questions.question: Why did the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation ask participants to complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exploration, while the questionnaire for environmental presence was completed only after exploration?
questions.reference_answer: The evaluation aimed to measure usability aspects such as presence and comfort and to identify potential improvements by analyzing cybersickness symptoms. Presence is a psychological state measured by standard questionnaires, and the questionnaire for environmental presence was used as the presence measure after exploration. Because cybersickness depends on exposure, the simulator sickness questionnaire was completed before exploration and after the session so pre- and post-exposure scores could be compared to assess the tour's effect.

questions.question: How do the presence results and the Welch t-test finding on prior exposure explain the risk of prior virtual reality experience biasing the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?
questions.reference_answer: Twenty-one of the 27 participants had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output, and a pre-experiment training session can reduce or nullify such prior-experience bias. The presence measure gave mostly good results, and a Welch t-test revealed a statistically significant difference between users with and without prior exposure to digital or virtual tours, supporting that prior exposure helps users gain a better experience. Previous visitors gave more favorable presence ratings despite higher expectations, suggesting they felt comfortable with digital exploration, that the system reasonably well mimicked the physical island environment in its design elements, interaction, and implementation, and that the digital avatar was close to reality.

questions.question: What do the simulator sickness questionnaire box plots and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test together suggest about which parts of cybersickness the Majuli virtual tour affected?
questions.reference_answer: The box plots showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour did not generally induce cybersickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test found a statistically significant difference between pre- and post-exposure outcomes for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item. This indicates that the tour design had some effect on total sickness, with the oculomotor component possibly being affected.
